passage: In the robotics room after school, Irawati ma'am held out the camp form. “Seats close on Friday, Uma. You built the best arm in the club.” Uma smiled too quickly. “June is busy. Family things.” The form stayed on the desk. At home that evening nobody asked, because Uma had said nothing; Papa only remarked how nice it would be to have an extra pair of hands at the shop all month. Uma nodded and kept stacking notebooks. Through June, Uma counted stock with a tight jaw, answered in single words, and once shut the cash drawer so hard that a customer jumped. “What's wrong with you?” asked Papa. “Nothing.” The family thought the summer had gone smoothly. Irawati ma'am glanced at the empty chair on the camp list and wondered why Uma never explained.

qa.q: By which day did the camp seats close?
qa.a: On Friday.

qa.q: What was Uma feeling while counting stock in June?
qa.a: Resentment: the tight jaw, one-word answers and the slammed drawer show anger that was never spoken.

qa.q: What could Uma have done instead, and why might it work?
qa.a: Uma could have told Papa what the camp meant and asked what the shop really needed, because then the family could look for a way to meet both needs instead of losing one silently.

qa.q: How does the summer look to Papa?
qa.a: Papa believes it went smoothly and does not know Uma gave up something important, so he cannot understand the short temper.

grounding: A student gives up the camp silently to avoid conflict, resentment builds and the family never learns the cost.

subtype: Approach: pursuing the desire while ignoring the family [Pitfall]
passage: Day 3 of camp, 10 pm. I still can't believe I'm here. Today my team's line-following car finally stayed on the track and everyone cheered. I've told nobody at home; Mummy thinks I'm at my cousin Lokesh's, doing project work. It felt like freedom all morning. Then at lunch a text came from Lokesh: “Your mom has asked me three times where you are. I said I don't know. Don't do this to me.” Papa rang my phone twice and I let it ring. Someone also told me the shop turned away two big orders because nobody was at the counter. The car works fine. My stomach doesn't. I wanted this so badly that I never looked at anyone else. — Gargi

qa.q: What finally worked for Gargi's team on day three?
qa.a: Their line-following car finally stayed on the track.

qa.q: What is Gargi feeling at the end of the entry?
qa.a: Uneasy and guilty: Gargi's stomach is unsettled because the wanting was so strong that nobody else was considered.

qa.q: What could Gargi have done differently, and why?
qa.a: Gargi could have talked to the parents about the camp and the shop beforehand, because being open lets the family share the plan and keeps their trust.

qa.q: How might Lokesh feel about being asked where Gargi is?
qa.a: Lokesh is put in an awkward spot, asked to cover for something that Lokesh knew little about, which is why the text begs Gargi not to do this.

grounding: A student joins the camp secretly, ignoring the family's need, which breaks trust and leaves the shop uncovered.

passage: On Sunday after lunch Rajni put the camp brochure beside the shop ledger on the table. “Papa, before you say anything, let me show you why this matters, and then you tell me what June really looks like at the shop.” Yusuf raised his eyebrows. Rajni explained that the camp certificate counted for the science-college forms. Yusuf turned the ledger pages slowly. “The heavy weeks are only the last ten days of the month, when new stock comes in,” he said. Rajni blinked; the picture in Rajni's head had been the whole month. “And I did not know the certificate was for admissions,” Yusuf said. Neither had expected that. They wrote both sets of dates on one sheet and agreed to check the camp calendar together on Monday.

qa.q: When are the heavy weeks at the shop?
qa.a: The last ten days of the month, when new stock comes in.

qa.q: What did Rajni feel when Yusuf described the busy weeks?
qa.a: Surprise: Rajni blinked, because the busy time was much shorter than the whole month Rajni had imagined.

qa.q: Why did asking and listening work better than guessing?
qa.a: A written comparison of the real dates let both sides check the actual needs before deciding, instead of each assuming the worst.

qa.q: How does the talk look to Yusuf?
qa.a: Yusuf learns something new, that the certificate matters for admissions, and sees Rajni asking about the shop, so he has a reason to take the camp seriously.

grounding: A student explains what the camp means, asks what the shop needs and listens, so nobody is surprised.

passage: The registration link closed at nine the next morning, and the power had gone out, so the family sat around one lamp in the shop's back room. Jasleen had a pencil and the back of a bill. “Two evenings before camp I'll work the counter till closing,” she said. Her mother tapped the wall calendar. “And during?” “Cousin Thomas can come. He said he's free that fortnight.” Papa raised an eyebrow. “Accounts?” “I'll fill the daily sheet on my phone every night from camp. Ten minutes.” Papa counted on his fingers: two evenings, a cousin, a nightly sheet. “Neither of us gets everything we wanted,” he said. “But nobody loses everything.” Jasleen hugged her mother, then rang Thomas by torchlight.

qa.q: How will Jasleen handle the accounts during camp?
qa.a: She will fill the daily sheet on her phone every night, about ten minutes.

qa.q: What might Jasleen have felt when Papa said nobody loses everything?
qa.a: Relief and gratitude: she hugged her mother and rang her cousin at once.

qa.q: What could the family try if Thomas could not come, and why?
qa.a: They could ask a neighbour's teenager or shorten the shifts, because the aim is to keep the counter covered without dropping the camp.

qa.q: How does the deal look to Thomas?
qa.a: Thomas is being asked to give up a fortnight of free time, so he would want proper notice and clear hours; his ready yes suggests he wants to help.

grounding: A family agrees two evenings of work, a cousin's cover and online accounts so both needs are partly met.

subtype: Approach: consulting an elder for perspective [Action]
passage: Thursday. Went to Ammamma's room after dinner with the camp form still in my bag. She asked why I looked like a wet cat. I told her Papa wants me at the shop in June. She was quiet, then said, “At sixteen I gave up my place at the teachers' college to help my father in the fields.” I hadn't known that. “I don't regret helping him, kanna. I regret never telling him what it cost me. He would have found some way.” She said duty and growing up aren't two doors where you must close one; over a whole life you keep walking back and forth between them. She told me to say my piece first, and decide after. I feel steadier. Tomorrow I'll talk to Papa. (Ammamma's tea is still terrible.) — Pallavi

qa.q: What did Ammamma give up at sixteen?
qa.a: Her place at the teachers' college, to help her father in the fields.

qa.q: What does Ammamma feel about her old choice?
qa.a: Regret, not for helping her father, but for never telling him what it cost her.

qa.q: What could Pallavi do next, and why?
qa.a: Pallavi could talk to Papa openly before deciding, since Ammamma's story shows that hiding the cost takes away the family's chance to find another way.

qa.q: How might Papa see Pallavi's silence if it continued?
qa.a: Papa might assume everything is fine and never see what Pallavi would give up, just as Ammamma's father never knew.

grounding: A student consults a grandmother, who shares her similar choice and its regrets, giving a longer view.

subtype: Approach: sleeping on it before choosing [Thinking]
passage: “Well? Camp or shop?” Papa asked over dinner, and Anjali put down her roti. “Tomorrow, please. Let me answer tomorrow.” That night she lay on the charpai listening to the crickets. If I say camp, Amma will look hurt. If I say shop, I'll hate the counter all June. Why do I keep seeing Papa's face when I think about camp? Around midnight the reason floated up: it wasn't the shop she feared, it was the moment Papa and Amma looked let down. In the morning, while Hansa, her mother, poured tea in the yard, Anjali said, “I'm scared you'll think I'm ungrateful.” Amma set the cup down. “Then tell me what you want, and we'll talk.”

qa.q: When did Anjali ask to give her answer?
qa.a: The next day; she asked to answer tomorrow.

qa.q: What did Anjali realise she was most afraid of?
qa.a: Disappointing her parents, more than losing the camp or working at the counter.

qa.q: What could Anjali do to prepare for the talk, and why?
qa.a: She could jot down what the camp means to her and what she can offer the shop, so the fear of letting them down does not force a plain yes or no.

qa.q: How might Hansa feel hearing Anjali say she is scared of seeming ungrateful?
qa.a: Hansa may be touched and relieved to hear the real worry, which makes an open talk easier 🙂.

grounding: A student postpones the answer by a night and discovers the bigger fear was disappointing the parents.

subtype: Approach: reviewing the compromise after a month [Revision]
passage: A month after the family had agreed the new schedule, they sat in the shop after closing with the tea kettle between them and the tally notebook open. Papa asked each person to say what was working. Parul said the Tuesday evening shift was fine but tiring. Sachin, Parul's brother, admitted the same slot clashed with his coaching class. Mother slid the notebook over: the daily sheets Parul filled from camp had made the evening tally match for the first time in years. They swapped, so Sachin took Saturday mornings and Parul took Tuesdays. Then Papa thanked each of them by name, for the counter, the sheets and the patience. Parul stacked the cups a little more lightly than usual. They wrote the next review on the calendar for a month ahead.

qa.q: Why did the Tuesday shift need to change?
qa.a: It clashed with Sachin's coaching class.

qa.q: What might Parul have felt when Papa thanked each person by name?
qa.a: Seen and valued, which makes the arrangement feel fair instead of a burden.

qa.q: What else could the family do to keep the arrangement fair, and why?
qa.a: Set the next review a month ahead, because exams and stock change and a regular check lets them adjust before resentment grows.

qa.q: How does the plan look to Sachin?
qa.a: A shift he did not choose had squeezed his coaching time, so the swap shows that his time matters too.

grounding: A month on, the family reviews the schedule, adjusts shifts and makes sure each person's effort is seen.

subtype: Approach: accepting a real limit and deferring the desire [Revision]
passage: Every option had been tried. The camp ran the same two weeks as the winter stock rush, Cousin Ravi was away, and the shorter programme in the city was full. Lalit sat with his father Vikas at the counter after closing, pushing a pencil back and forth. “So we can't,” Lalit said. “Not this year.” Vikas nodded, and a heavy quiet filled the shop. Then Lalit pulled over a fresh sheet and wrote a heading: NEXT YEAR. Under it he wrote: apply the day registration opens in January; ask Mr Nair for a recommendation letter; ask Papa to plan the shop cover for that fortnight early. “It's late, not lost,” he said. Vikas read the list twice. “Put my name next to the third one,” he said.

qa.q: When will Lalit apply next year?
qa.a: The day registration opens in January.

qa.q: How does Lalit feel about skipping this year, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Disappointed but steady: he pushes the pencil around in silence, then writes a plan and calls the camp late, not lost.

qa.q: What else could Lalit do to keep the goal alive this year, and why?
qa.a: He could build a small robot project at home or join a free online club, since practice through the year keeps his skills growing until the next camp.

qa.q: How does the plan look to Vikas?
qa.a: Vikas sees his son accept a hard limit without blaming anyone, and the list gives him a concrete part to play, so it becomes a shared goal.

grounding: When no option works this year, a student skips the camp but writes a plan to apply next year with parental support.

passage: Exams began in three weeks, so Noor had a single Sunday and two evenings to spare. On the kitchen table he wrote his skills: fixing phones, drawing, teaching basic maths. His sister Vandana, home from college, read over his shoulder. “Now ask which ones are allowed for someone your age, and safe,” she said. Noor crossed out the phone stall in the market: it wanted full days and ran till nine at night. Drawing wedding-card sketches at home on Sundays stayed. Maths lessons for the neighbour's child after school, in daylight, in their own building, stayed too. “Show it to Mum before you say yes to anybody,” Vandana added. Noor sighed at the crossed-out line; he had liked the phones best. Then he copied the two remaining lines onto a clean page.

qa.q: Which skills did Noor list?
qa.a: Fixing phones, drawing and teaching basic maths.

qa.q: How did Noor feel about crossing out the phone stall?
qa.a: Disappointed but sensible: he liked the phones best, yet accepted that full days and late hours did not suit school or his age.

qa.q: What could Noor do to test an option before committing, and why?
qa.a: He could start with one small trial, such as tutoring the neighbour's child for a month, because it shows whether the work fits around exams before he takes on more.

qa.q: How might Vandana see his plan?
qa.a: Vandana, who asked him to check what suits his age and to show Mum, would likely feel reassured that he thought about safety and school before taking on paid work.

grounding: A sixteen-year-old lists skills and checks which suit his age, are safe and fit around school.

subtype: Approach: checking legal and safety limits with parents [Action]
passage:
Maria: Papa, can I ask about the Saturday job at the bakery near school? 🙂
Arnab: Tell me the details first.
Maria: Ten to two, packing boxes and helping at the counter. Not the ovens. Mrs Pinto said she'll pay weekly.
Arnab: Daytime, inside a shop we know. Good. What about school hours?
Maria: Saturdays only. Homework Sunday morning as usual.
Arnab: I'll ask the school office what the rules are for your age before you say yes. Don't accept anything yet.
Maria: Okay. Should I come along when you visit her?
Arnab: Yes, and Mummy too. We'll all look at the timings together.
Maria: Thank you for not saying no straight away 👍
Arnab: I'm glad you asked me first.

qa.q: What will Maria do at the bakery?
qa.a: Pack boxes and help at the counter, not work at the ovens.

qa.q: What might Maria be feeling when thanking Arnab for not saying no straight away?
qa.a: Relief and a bit of hope: Maria expected a quick refusal and is glad Papa is listening.

qa.q: What else could Maria do to keep the plan safe, and why?
qa.a: Maria could bring the bakery owner's written timings and duties to the family visit, because clear written details make it easier for everyone to check the work suits Maria's age.

qa.q: How does the plan look to Arnab?
qa.a: Arnab is glad to be asked first, and checking the place, daylight hours and the school's rules lets him say yes with confidence rather than worry.

grounding: A student discusses the job with parents, confirms it is age-appropriate, in daylight and safe, and checks the rules first.
